environments.label: Space station (low Earth orbit)
environments.support: Near-continuous contact with flight surgeons. An emergency return to Earth is possible within hours.
environments.escalation: Contact the flight surgeon now through mission control, or at the next private medical conference if it is not urgent.

environments.label: Deep-space transit
environments.commsDelay: Seconds to over 20 minutes, growing with distance
environments.support: No quick return. The medical kit and the Crew Medical Officer (CMO) are your main resources.
environments.escalation: The CMO leads the response. Send a health report to the flight surgeon and keep following the checklist while you wait for a reply.

environments.label: Lunar base
environments.support: Return to Earth takes several days. Lunar dust can irritate the eyes and lungs.
environments.escalation: Call the flight surgeon directly. Near real-time conversation is possible.

environments.label: Mars base
environments.support: No return for months. The crew must assess and treat on their own.
environments.escalation: The CMO leads treatment. Send the health report to Earth now; a reply can take up to about 45 minutes round trip.

environments.label: Pressurized rover sortie
environments.support: Limited medical kit and no full exercise equipment until you are back at base.
environments.escalation: Notify the base, pause the traverse, and consider returning early.

regions.label: Brain & Behavior
regions.description: Sleep and mood are early warning signs of the strain that isolation, confinement, and disrupted day–night cycles put on behavioral health.

regions.label: Immune System
regions.description: Spaceflight can weaken immune function and reactivate dormant viruses. Body temperature is the simplest daily proxy for infection or inflammation.

regions.label: Lungs
regions.description: Cabin atmosphere (CO2 buildup, dust on planetary surfaces) affects how well blood carries oxygen.

regions.label: Heart
regions.description: In microgravity, body fluids shift toward the head and the heart is under less load, which over time leads to cardiovascular deconditioning.

regions.label: Metabolism
regions.description: Inactivity, diet changes, and stress hormones can push blood glucose regulation toward insulin resistance.

regions.label: Bones & Muscles
regions.description: Without exercise countermeasures, weight-bearing bones can lose about 1–1.5% of their mineral density per month in microgravity, and muscles atrophy.

indicators.label: Resting heart rate
indicators.howToMeasure: Right after waking, sit still for 5 minutes, then count your pulse for 60 seconds or read it from the wearable sensor.
indicators.whyItMatters: Resting heart rate that keeps rising can point to deconditioning, dehydration, illness, or poor sleep.

guidance.nominal: Within the expected range. Keep up your scheduled exercise.

low.caution: Lower than usual. If you feel dizzy or faint, sit or anchor yourself and re-measure in 15 minutes.
low.critical: Very low heart rate. Stop activity, re-measure, and notify the Crew Medical Officer (CMO) and flight surgeon.

high.caution: Elevated at rest. Hydrate, rest for 15 minutes, and re-measure. Check for fever or stress.
high.critical: Heart rate is high at rest. Stop activity, re-measure, and notify the CMO and flight surgeon now.

indicators.label: Systolic blood pressure
indicators.howToMeasure: Sit (or restrain yourself) with your arm supported at heart level. Put the cuff on your bare upper arm, rest for 5 minutes, then take two readings 1 minute apart.
indicators.whyItMatters: Fluid shifts and vascular changes in spaceflight can change blood pressure regulation.

low.caution: Low blood pressure. Increase fluid intake and watch for light-headedness.
low.critical: Very low blood pressure. Lie down or anchor yourself, re-measure, and notify the CMO.

high.caution: Elevated. Cut back on sodium, re-measure tomorrow, and log any headache.
high.critical: High blood pressure. Re-measure in 5 minutes; if it is still high, notify the flight surgeon.

indicators.label: Diastolic blood pressure
indicators.howToMeasure: Recorded in the same cuff reading as systolic pressure (the lower number).
indicators.whyItMatters: Diastolic pressure shows the load on your blood vessels between heartbeats.

low.caution: Low diastolic pressure. Hydrate and re-measure.
low.critical: Very low diastolic pressure. Re-measure and notify the CMO.

high.caution: Elevated. Re-measure tomorrow at the same time of day.
high.critical: High diastolic pressure. Re-measure in 5 minutes; if it is still high, notify the flight surgeon.

indicators.label: Fasting blood glucose
indicators.howToMeasure: Before breakfast, after at least 8 hours without food. Clean your fingertip, lance it, and read a drop with the glucometer.
indicators.whyItMatters: Physical inactivity and stress hormones in spaceflight can reduce insulin sensitivity.

low.caution: Low glucose. Eat 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and re-check in 15 minutes.
low.critical: Severe low glucose. Take 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate now, tell a crewmate, and notify the CMO.

high.caution: Above the fasting target. Confirm you were fasting, review your meals, and re-check tomorrow.
high.critical: High glucose. Re-check, drink water, and notify the flight surgeon.

indicators.label: Body temperature
indicators.howToMeasure: Use the same thermometer, at the same site and the same time each day, at least 30 minutes after exercise or meals.
indicators.whyItMatters: Core body temperature tends to run slightly higher during long missions, so a fever can point to infection or immune changes.

low.caution: Below normal. Check your clothing layers and cabin temperature, then re-measure.
low.critical: Low body temperature. Warm up and notify the CMO.

high.caution: Slightly elevated. Rest, hydrate, and re-measure in 2 hours. Watch for other symptoms.
high.critical: Fever. Rest, hydrate, isolate if possible, and notify the CMO and flight surgeon.

indicators.label: Blood oxygen (SpO₂)
indicators.howToMeasure: Clip the pulse oximeter onto a warm finger, keep still for 30 seconds, then read the steady value.
indicators.whyItMatters: Low oxygen saturation can mean breathing problems or an issue with the cabin atmosphere.

low.caution: Slightly low. Warm your hands, re-measure, and check the cabin CO₂ readout.
low.critical: Low oxygen saturation. Move to a well-ventilated module and notify the CMO immediately.

indicators.label: Cabin CO₂
indicators.howToMeasure: Read the CO₂ partial pressure (ppCO₂) for the module where you spend most of the day. In a sleep station or crowded module, take a reading with the handheld CO₂ monitor.
indicators.whyItMatters: NASA’s analysis of ISS data found that each 1 mmHg rise in CO₂ almost doubles the odds of a headache. CO₂ collects where air doesn’t move.

guidance.nominal: At or below NASA’s CO₂ target for this environment.

high.caution: Above NASA’s target. Turn up airflow, avoid crowding into one module, note any headache, and check again in a few hours.
high.critical: Above 6 mmHg, the level at which NASA consults flight surgeons. Move to a well-ventilated module, report headache or lethargy, and tell the ground.

indicators.label: Sleep duration
indicators.howToMeasure: Log your total hours of sleep last night, or read it from the actigraphy watch.
indicators.whyItMatters: Seeing many sunrises a day, noise, and workload often keep crews below 6 hours of sleep, which hurts mood, reaction time, and immunity.

guidance.nominal: Good sleep. Keep your sleep schedule consistent.

low.caution: Short sleep. Limit screens before bed, use eye shades and earplugs, and protect your sleep window tonight.
low.critical: Severe sleep deficit. Avoid critical tasks if you can and talk with the CMO about your schedule.

high.caution: Longer sleep than usual can be a sign of illness or low mood. Check your other indicators.
high.critical: Excessive sleep. Talk with the CMO.

indicators.label: Mood self-rating
indicators.howToMeasure: Rate how you feel today: 1 = very low, 3 = okay, 5 = great. Be honest; this log stays private to you.
indicators.whyItMatters: Isolation, confinement, and distance from family wear on behavioral health over long missions.

guidance.nominal: Feeling good. Keep taking personal time and staying in touch with family.

low.caution: Mood is lower than usual. Schedule a private call home, take a break, or talk with a crewmate.
low.critical: Mood is very low. Please request a private conference with the flight surgeon or psychologist.

indicators.label: Exercise countermeasures
indicators.howToMeasure: Log your total minutes of resistance and aerobic exercise today (treadmill, cycle ergometer, resistive device).
indicators.whyItMatters: About 2 hours of exercise a day is the main protection against bone and muscle loss in reduced gravity.

low.caution: Below the daily target. Add a resistance session to protect bone density.
low.critical: Well below target. Talk with ground fitness support (ASCR) about rescheduling sessions.
